Egypt. A transcontinental country spanning northeastern Africa and the Sinai Peninsula of southwestern Asia, centered on the valley and delta of the Nile River. Home to one of the world's earliest great civilizations, which flourished for over three millennia and left indelible marks on architecture, writing, and religion, Egypt remains a major cultural and geopolitical hub in the Middle East. The country is roughly ninety-seven percent desert, making the Nile's narrow fertile corridor the lifeblood of its population.

Egypt is bounded by the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the Red Sea to the east. The Suez Canal, one of the world's most strategically vital waterways, connects these two seas and crosses Egyptian territory. Ancient Egypt emerged around thirty one hundred BCE with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under the First Dynasty and lasted until Rome's conquest in thirty BCE, spanning roughly three thousand years of continuous civilization. The Egyptian pyramids, particularly the Great Pyramid of Giza, were built as monumental tombs for pharaohs during the Old Kingdom from circa twenty-six eighty-six to twenty one eighty-one BCE. They remain among the world's most recognizable structures.

Hieroglyphics, the ancient Egyptian writing system combining logographic and alphabetic elements, was used for nearly thirty-five hundred years until replaced by Coptic after Roman conquest. The Nile River is the world's longest river, flowing northward through Egypt for over six thousand six hundred kilometers. Ancient Egyptian civilization was entirely dependent on its annual flooding cycles, which the Aswan High Dam, completed in nineteen seventy, now controls. Cleopatra VII, from sixty-nine to thirty BCE, was the last active pharaoh of Egypt. She was renowned for her intelligence, her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, and her linguistic abilities in as many as nine languages.

Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world with over one hundred million inhabitants. Islam is the predominant religion, with Coptic Christianity as the largest minority. The Suez Canal, opened in eighteen sixty-nine, redirected world maritime trade and made Egypt a strategic chokepoint. Its seizure in nineteen fifty-six by President Gamal Abdel Nasser triggered an international crisis.
